title: What are the Spring Kafka `AckMode`s — `RECORD` (commit after each record), `BATCH` (commit after the whole `poll()` batch, the default), `TIME`, `COUNT`, `COUNT_TIME`, and `MANUAL`/`MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` (you call `Acknowledgment.acknowledge()`) — when do you use manual acknowledgment, and why does commit-after-processing give at-least-once semantics?
shortTitle: What are the Spring Kafka AckModes, when do you use manual acknowledgment, and why does commit-after-processing give at-least-once?

s1_definition.profdef: In Spring Kafka an `AckMode` controls when the listener container commits consumer offsets, which is how Kafka remembers how far a consumer has read. `RECORD` commits after each record, `BATCH` commits once after the whole `poll()` batch is processed and is the default, `TIME` commits on a time interval, `COUNT` after a number of records, `COUNT_TIME` on whichever of count or time comes first, and `MANUAL` and `MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` hand control to your code through an injected `Acknowledgment` object that you call with `acknowledge()`. Because the offset is committed only after your business logic has run successfully, a crash between processing and committing causes a redelivery, which is precisely the at-least-once guarantee.
s1_definition.analogy: The offset is a bookmark in a ledger that says how many transactions the clerk at National Bank of India has already posted. The AckMode decides when the clerk moves the bookmark forward. `RECORD` moves it after every single posting, `BATCH` moves it once after finishing the whole tray, and `MANUAL` means the clerk only moves it when they personally confirm the posting is safely in the ledger. If the clerk posts Rajesh's transfer but faints before moving the bookmark, a new clerk starts from the old bookmark and posts it again — the money is never lost, but it might be posted twice, so the ledger must tolerate a repeat.
s1_definition.oneliner: The AckMode is when the offset bookmark moves, and committing only after successful processing is what makes delivery at-least-once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Spring Kafka an `AckMode` controls when the listener container commits consumer offsets, which is how Kafka remembers how far a consumer has read. `RECORD` commits after each record, `BATCH` commits once after the whole `poll()` batch is processed and is the default, `TIME` commits on a time interval, `COUNT` after a number of records, `COUNT_TIME` on whichever of count or time comes first, and `MANUAL` and `MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` hand control to your code through an injected `Acknowledgment` object that you call with `acknowledge()`. Because the offset is committed only after your business logic has run successfully, a crash between processing and committing causes a redelivery, which is precisely the at-least-once guarantee.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The offset is a bookmark in a ledger that says how many transactions the clerk at National Bank of India has already posted. The AckMode decides when the clerk moves the bookmark forward. `RECORD` moves it after every single posting, `BATCH` moves it once after finishing the whole tray, and `MANUAL` means the clerk only moves it when they personally confirm the posting is safely in the ledger. If the clerk posts Rajesh's transfer but faints before moving the bookmark, a new clerk starts from the old bookmark and posts it again — the money is never lost, but it might be posted twice, so the ledger must tolerate a repeat.

**One line to remember:** The AckMode is when the offset bookmark moves, and committing only after successful processing is what makes delivery at-least-once.

sections.s2_technical:
An offset is Kafka's record of how far a consumer group has consumed each partition. Committing an offset of N means "I have safely processed everything up to N, restart me from N if I crash." If you commit before processing, you get at-most-once, because a crash after the commit but before the work loses the record. If you commit after processing, you get at-least-once, because a crash after the work but before the commit replays the record. Spring Kafka's AckModes are different policies for exactly when that commit happens relative to your method running.

`RECORD` mode commits after each individual record's listener call returns successfully, giving the tightest redelivery window at the cost of more commit traffic. `BATCH`, the default, waits until every record returned by one `poll()` has been processed and then commits the highest offset of that batch in one go, which is efficient but means a failure midway through a batch can replay the earlier successful records too. `TIME` commits whenever a configured interval elapses, `COUNT` after a configured number of records, and `COUNT_TIME` whenever either threshold is hit first; these are throughput-oriented policies that trade a larger possible replay window for fewer commits.

`MANUAL` and `MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` put you in charge. Spring injects an `Acknowledgment` into your listener and you decide when to commit: `public void onTxn(TxnEvent e, Acknowledgment ack) { settlementService.settle(e); ack.acknowledge(); }`. With `MANUAL` the acknowledgement is queued and committed when the batch completes, while `MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` commits right away on the consumer thread. You use manual acknowledgement when the commit must be tied to a side effect succeeding, for example only committing after the database write and the downstream publish both succeed, so that if the database write throws, you do not acknowledge and Kafka redelivers the event for a genuine retry.

The reason commit-after-processing is at-least-once is a simple ordering argument. The container calls your method, your method does the work, and only then does the offset advance. If the process dies at any point before the commit lands, the broker still has the old offset, so when the consumer restarts or the partition is reassigned after a rebalance, it re-reads from that old offset and your method runs again for records it had already processed. Kafka cannot give you exactly-once on the consume-and-act side by offsets alone, so the senior takeaway is that at-least-once plus idempotent processing, meaning you make repeated processing of the same event harmless using an idempotency key or a dedup table, is how you get effectively-once behaviour in a bank. A further nuance is that even `BATCH` mode is at-least-once, not exactly-once, and choosing `RECORD` or manual only shrinks the size of the replay window, it does not eliminate replays.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that the settlement consumer must never lose a transaction, but with naive offset handling it can either lose events or replay them in confusing ways.

Problem 1 — if the consumer commits the offset the moment it reads an event and then crashes before writing the settlement to the database, that transaction is gone forever, because the bookmark already moved past it. The bank cannot tolerate a lost transfer. This is why the team never commits before processing; they commit after, which gives at-least-once and guarantees no event is dropped.

Problem 2 — with manual acknowledgement, the team wants the offset to advance only when both the database write and the downstream notification publish have succeeded. If the database is briefly down, the listener should not acknowledge, so Kafka redelivers the same event and it is retried cleanly. This is exactly `MANUAL_IMMEDIATE` tied to successful side effects.

Problem 3 — because at-least-once means the same event can be processed twice after a crash, the settlement write must be idempotent so a replay does not double-post Rajesh's transfer. The demo shows an idempotent store keyed by transaction id so a redelivery is a harmless no-op.

The code will define a TxnEvent, an `Acknowledgment` abstraction, a `SettlementConsumer` that processes then acknowledges, an idempotent `SettlementStore`, and a `ContainerSimulator` that feeds events, simulates a crash between processing and acknowledging one event, and then replays from the last committed offset to prove at-least-once with idempotent safety. The demo step is: process three events, crash right after settling the second but before acknowledging, restart from the last commit, and show the second event redelivered and safely deduplicated.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE settlements (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,      -- idempotency key, redelivery = no-op
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    settled_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Idempotent insert: redelivered event does not double-post.
-- INSERT INTO settlements (...) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (txn_id) DO NOTHING;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      enable-auto-commit: false   # container manages commits, not auto-commit
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
    listener:
      ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE  # we call ack.acknowledge() after side effects succeed
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one partition holding three transactions for Rajesh and Priya, consumed with manual immediate acknowledgement, where the offset is a bookmark starting at index zero.

Step 1: The container reads TXN-1 at offset zero and calls the consumer, which posts the settlement to the idempotent store and then calls acknowledge, moving the committed bookmark to one. The data is now safely in the store and the bookmark reflects it.

Step 2: The container reads TXN-2 at offset one and the consumer posts it to the store successfully. But the process crashes before the commit is actually flushed to the broker, so the committed bookmark is rolled back to one. The settlement for TXN-2 is in the store, but Kafka still thinks it has not been consumed.

Step 3: The consumer restarts. Kafka hands it the partition starting from the last committed offset, which is one, so it re-reads TXN-2. This is at-least-once in action: the event is delivered again because the commit never landed.

Step 4: The consumer processes TXN-2 a second time, but the idempotent store sees the transaction id already posted and ignores it as a harmless no-op, so there is no double-posting of Rajesh's money. The bookmark now advances to two.

Step 5: The consumer reads TXN-3 at offset two, posts Priya's settlement, acknowledges, and the bookmark moves to three. Consumption is complete.

Step 6: The final output shows TXN-2 processed twice but stored once, proving at-least-once plus idempotency gives effectively-once.

```
2026-10-24 22:40:05 [INFO] === Run 1: crash AFTER settling TXN-2 but BEFORE acknowledging ===
2026-10-24 22:40:05 [INFO] posted settlement txn=TXN-1 account=SAV2001 amount=Rs.20000
2026-10-24 22:40:05 [INFO] posted settlement txn=TXN-2 account=SAV2001 amount=Rs.30000
2026-10-24 22:40:05 [SEVERE] CRASH after processing txn=TXN-2 but before commit flushed; committedOffset=1
2026-10-24 22:40:05 [INFO] === Run 2: restart from last committed offset (TXN-2) ===
2026-10-24 22:40:05 [INFO] restarting from committedOffset=1
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Partition: [TXN-1 @0] [TXN-2 @1] [TXN-3 @2]   committed bookmark = 0
    │
    ▼
  container reads @0 → consumer.onTxn(TXN-1, ack)
    │ store.settle(TXN-1) → ack.acknowledge() → bookmark = 1
    ▼
  container reads @1 → consumer.onTxn(TXN-2, ack)
    │ store.settle(TXN-2)
    │ CRASH before commit flush → bookmark stays 1
    ▼
  ─── restart / rebalance ───
  container reads @1 again (at-least-once redelivery)
    │ store.settle(TXN-2) → ALREADY POSTED → no-op (idempotent)
    │ ack.acknowledge() → bookmark = 2
    ▼
  container reads @2 → consumer.onTxn(TXN-3, ack) → bookmark = 3
    ▼
  Result: TXN-2 delivered twice, stored once = effectively-once
```

```
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> Acknowledgment  (+ acknowledge())               │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: offset bookmark for one record ──────────────────

  [READ @N] ──process ok──→ [PROCESSED] ──ack──→ [COMMITTED @N+1]
      │                          │
      │                          │ crash before commit
      ▼                          ▼
  (nothing)                  [REDELIVERED @N] → idempotent no-op → [COMMITTED]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. container.run(crashAfterIndex=1)
  2.   → onTxn(TXN-1) → store.settle → ack → bookmark=1
  3.   → onTxn(TXN-2) → store.settle → CRASH before flush → bookmark=1
  4. container.resume()
  5.   → onTxn(TXN-2) → store.settle → duplicate, no-op
  6.   → ack → bookmark=2 → onTxn(TXN-3) → bookmark=3
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In Spring Kafka the AckMode decides exactly when the listener container commits consumer offsets, and the offset is simply Kafka's bookmark of how far a consumer group has read a partition. RECORD commits after every individual record, BATCH commits once after the whole poll batch and is the default, TIME and COUNT and COUNT_TIME commit on an interval or a count or whichever comes first, and MANUAL and MANUAL_IMMEDIATE hand the decision to your code through an injected Acknowledgment object that you call explicitly.

I reach for manual acknowledgement whenever the commit has to be tied to a side effect succeeding. In the settlement service at National Bank of India, the listener wrote the settlement to the database and only then called acknowledge, so if the database was briefly unavailable the method did not acknowledge, the offset did not advance, and Kafka redelivered the event for a clean retry. Manual immediate commits right away on the consumer thread, which gives the smallest redelivery window, while plain manual defers the commit to the end of the batch.

The reason committing after processing gives at-least-once is just the order of operations. The container runs my method, my method does the work, and only then does the offset move. If the process dies at any moment before the commit lands, the broker still holds the old offset, so on restart or after a rebalance the consumer re-reads those records and processes them again. That means a record is never lost, but it can be delivered more than once.

The senior point I always add is that at-least-once is the realistic guarantee for the consume-and-act side, and the way a bank makes it safe is to make processing idempotent. In our service the settlements table had the transaction id as its primary key with an insert-on-conflict-do-nothing, so a redelivery of Rajesh's transfer was a harmless no-op and his money was never posted twice. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing is how you achieve effectively-once in practice, and changing the AckMode only shrinks or widens the replay window, it never removes replays entirely.

keyPoints: At-most-once: fire and forget — may lose messages
At-least-once: retry on failure — may duplicate
